analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder to challenge an existing patent through the Patent Office's cheaper review process.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 3 cosponsors and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up; it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules for inter partes review, a cheaper, faster way to ask the Patent Office to cancel an issued patent. Only people already sued or formally charged with infringement could ask for a review, the challenger would have to prove the patent invalid by clear and convincing evidence (a higher bar), and once a review is started the challenger generally could not raise the same arguments in court. It would also let the Patent Office keep and spend its fees without a separate annual appropriation from Congress, and would extend discounted filing fees to universities and nonprofits that hold patents for them.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of issued patents, especially large patent-portfolio holders such as brand-name drug companies, patent-licensing firms, and universities, gain because their patents become harder and more expensive to invalidate. Defendants in infringement suits lose their cheapest defense tool, and the cost of weeding out bad patents shifts onto them and, ultimately, consumers who pay more for patented goods.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Holders of issued patents, especially large portfolios

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars anyone who has not been sued for or charged with infringing a patent from petitioning for an inter partes review, ending the current rule that any person may petition.
It raises the challenger's burden of proof in inter partes review to clear and convincing evidence, the stricter standard used in federal court, instead of the preponderance standard now applied.
Once an inter partes review is instituted, the challenger may not raise the same validity challenges again in district court or at the International Trade Commission, forcing a single forum.

The bill responds to what its findings call strategic, repetitive post-grant proceedings used to depress stock prices and harass patent owners, and adds timing limits, estoppel rules, and panel-conduct requirements at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board.

It ends fee diversion by making all Patent Office fees available to the Office without further annual appropriations, and gives universities and nonprofits holding patents for them discounted patent fees.

analysis.who_pays: Companies and individuals accused of patent infringement, most often technology and product manufacturers and generic drug makers, lose the Patent Office review as a relatively low-cost way to knock out weak patents, and consumers bear the knock-on cost of stronger, longer-lasting patents in the prices of patented goods.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies accused of infringement, and consumers

drawbacks.text: The standing restriction means a company that sees a bad patent coming, but has not yet been sued, cannot use the Patent Office's cheaper review to clear it away; it must wait to be sued and litigate in federal court, where the cost of a validity fight is far higher.

Raising the burden of proof to clear and convincing evidence makes invalidating a wrongly granted patent substantially harder, which shifts the cost of correcting examiner mistakes from the Patent Office onto defendants and courts, and can keep weak patents in force that block competition and raise prices.

The single-forum and estoppel rules would strip challengers of the ability to press the same arguments in a second forum, a meaningful loss of flexibility even for people who agree the current system invites repetitive petitions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has some defensible fixes: ending fee diversion gives the Patent Office stable funding, timing limits cut delay, and limits on repetitive petitions address a real harassment problem. But its central changes — who may petition and to what standard of proof — would make the review process, the main low-cost check on wrongly granted patents, dramatically less available and less effective. The beneficiaries are concentrated patent owners; the costs fall on defendants and on consumers through stronger patent monopolies.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never scheduled a markup or vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Ken Buck introduced the PREVAIL Act in the House on June 27, 2023.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill had 3 cosponsors, one Democrat and two Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, companies that use inter partes review to knock out weak patents keep that cheaper tool, and patent owners gain nothing beyond the status quo. The beneficiaries of the inaction are the defendant-side industries that rely on the review process and, indirectly, consumers who benefit from bad patents being weeded out.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny: a Republican sponsor, one Democratic and two Republican cosponsors, no committee action, and no recorded votes of any kind.

industries.industry: Holders of issued patents (brand-name drug makers, patent-licensing firms, large IP portfolios)
industries.note: The bill makes issued patents harder to cancel by limiting who can petition, raising the proof standard, and barring repeat challenges, so patent owners keep exclusion rights longer. The cost lands on defendants and on consumers, who pay more for patented drugs and products while bad patents stay in force.

industries.industry: Technology and product manufacturers and generic drug makers facing infringement claims
industries.note: These companies would lose the Patent Office review as a relatively cheap way to invalidate weak patents: they could not petition unless already sued or charged, and would face a clear-and-convincing burden. Their litigation costs rise, which shows up in consumer prices.

industries.industry: Universities and nonprofits that hold patents
industries.note: The bill extends discounted filing fees to institutions of higher education and to nonprofits holding patents on their behalf, lowering the cost of building university patent portfolios.

Ending fee diversion lets the Office keep and spend all fees it collects without annual congressional appropriation, giving it stable, self-directed funding drawn from patent and trademark applicants.
